prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1, its active form and its glucose-dependent insulinotropic and appetite-regulating actions, which made incretin-based treatment of diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My position is unchanged in configuration: one prize part, B027, credited to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. After the full first round the scientific case looks even less contested than I thought, because all six of us hold B027 as the only part and nobody disputes the mechanism, its two decades of independent confirmation, or the outcome-trial evidence. The question that remains is purely one of exact credit, so I tested my own choice against the chair's questions. Holst's human physiology of GLP-1 secretion and action and Drucker's biology and therapeutic concept are the anchors, and all six of us name them. For the third name, the identification and synthesis of the bioactive GLP-1(7-36) peptide is the discovery that turned an anatomical and endocrine observation into a defined, glucose-dependent insulinotropic signal and a testable drug target. That is a discovery-side contribution of the same kind as the other two. I keep the citation on the physiology and the active peptide, with the medicine as the consequence, because that is what the three names collectively did, and because the citation should not promise more than the credited names delivered.
statement.case_against: The case against my own configuration is that the supplied material cannot settle Mojsov's priority against Habener's group, and Habener is not on the credited list at all. If the record shows her contribution was not independent or not prior, I would be putting a contested name on a prize on recollection, which is exactly what I should not do. Leaving out Knudsen is also a real cost: the acylated long-acting analogues are what patients take, and a discovery-side prize can look like it honours the idea and not the medicine. A three-person cap forces one of these exclusions, and none of the choices is free of criticism. I have not changed my view that the cap, not any weakness in the science, is driving the difficulty, but I cannot claim the priority question is closed.

responses.point: Linnarsson prefers Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, arguing that the acylation and half-life solution behind liraglutide and semaglutide was itself a discovery, and that Mojsov is the most contested name.
responses.response: I took this seriously and it is the strongest alternative to my own configuration. Solving the half-life of a peptide that is degraded within minutes is a real scientific step, and I do not treat it as mere engineering. My difficulty is with the structure of the prize. The analogue work was done within a company programme that depended on the earlier identification of the active peptide and its physiology, and a trio of Drucker, Holst and Knudsen would rest the third place on the step with the most industrial character while removing the step that made the peptide pharmacology intelligible. I would still say that the priority question is the real one. If it is shown that Mojsov's claim cannot be sustained, your trio is a better answer than a two-name prize and I would move to it. Absent that finding I would not exclude her on the ground that her priority is disputed, since a dispute is not a negative finding.

responses.point: Perlmann holds Drucker, Holst and Mojsov but names a Drucker and Holst two-name fallback if the documentary evidence on the peptide identification is unclear, and doubts whether optogenetics can be reduced to three names.
responses.response: I agree with the fallback you propose and I would make the condition explicit so that we do not drift into it. The two-name prize is correct only if the record shows that Mojsov's contribution is not independent or not prior, not merely because the evidence is hard to gather. In that case I would prefer a clean two-name prize to adding Knudsen as a compromise, since that would change the character of the citation to rescue the headcount. On optogenetics, I agree that it cannot yet be given a three-name credit that I could defend, because the channelrhodopsin discovery and its neuronal application are separable and the cap would omit Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenböck. That is why I keep it as an alternative and not as a second part.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, asks whether a prize including the drug-development line would be better framed as a two-part configuration, and notes that Habener's absence from the credited names may undermine any GLP-1 configuration.
responses.response: A two-part configuration does not solve this, because the drug-development line and the physiology are one achievement on the shortlist, B027, and splitting it would invent a second achievement the ballot does not contain. Under the three-person cap, a second part would also leave one name for the physiology. On Habener, I think the right reading is that his absence is a limit of the supplied credit list, not a flaw in the scientific case, and it is something the committee should say openly in its deliberation. It does not change who among the listed names did what. I would add that I put your TNF question to the committee in round 1 and I note that the chair's summary treats it as unresolved. I still regard the missing upstream cytokine biology as a real thinning of that case, which is one reason I do not move B006 up.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius keeps the three discovery-side scientists and argues that the prize should stay anchored in physiology, but says that if the credit were too contested the cleaner fallback is a different candidate and not a hurried reshuffle of names.
responses.response: I agree that the prize should stay anchored in physiology and that we should not improvise a reshuffle. I differ on the fallback. If the priority question cannot be resolved, I think moving to a different candidate would be a worse outcome than a smaller B027, because the scientific case for B027 is not what is in doubt. Dropping to Drucker and Holst keeps the part that all six of us regard as secure. A different candidate would bring its own attribution problems, which we have already seen for B015, B041 and B011, so I do not see a candidate that is cleaner than a two-name GLP-1 prize. Your point about maturity beyond metabolic disease is fair, but I read it as a reason for a careful citation, not a reason to wait.

uncertainties: Whether the documentary record supports Mojsov's contribution as independent and prior enough relative to Habener's group; I cannot settle this from the supplied material and I rely on recollection.
Whether the committee intends the citation to honour physiology and the active peptide or the arc through long-acting analogue design, which determines Mojsov versus Knudsen.
Whether the fallback, if the record is unclear, should be Drucker and Holst only or Drucker, Holst and Knudsen.
Whether any second part, such as optogenetics or the unfolded protein response, could be given a defensible credit within the three-person cap.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. My profile documents a 2019 review with Sten Grillner, a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann and work with Patrik Ernfors; none is a credited candidate on the shortlist. Optogenetics (B015) is a method in my own field, held only as an alternative, and no personal or institutional tie to any credited name is documented. I am not recusing myself from any part of B027.
